name: Colin Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, including anything you would keep separate from your public answer. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Colin, 43, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I'm still slower and less skilled than the experienced crew, so I prepare materials and help fit wiring with a senior worker checking me. Our firm pays at the higher end of the trade; that doesn't make me a better electrician than I actually am. Today I had to ask a younger worker to explain the drawing again before I marked a run in a shop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your household and your approach to unfamiliar tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a food warehouse, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have eight months of normal expenses saved and plenty of similar electrical firms nearby. I never use AI tools; I prefer the marked drawing and someone showing me the task until I've understood it. I believe in earning our way, keeping our word and family helping family, and I'd rather learn beside a tradesperson than take a chance on an expensive promise.

say: I'd welcome **less app chasing** and let the office make small invoice improvements.
I'd still need a **properly explained drawing** before attempting unfamiliar practical work under checks.
think: I expect our **wages and bills** to stay steady, with eight months of expenses saved and alternative firms nearby.
Being a **beginner** brings frustration without making every ordinary household bill feel threatening.
do: Continue the usual **supervised preparation** and fitting work now and through the first plateau year.
Keep the **drawing notebook** and request needed checks instead of buying new tools or leaving the wage.
feel: **Calm** about household money, with ordinary frustration at tasks that need another attempt.
S0.quote: Pride isn't much use if a fitting ends up wrong.
fieldNote: He separates **skill embarrassment** from financial insecurity, with a substantial reserve, high trade pay and many alternative firms supporting calm.
His **familiar methods** include repeated explanation and checks, without claiming a vocational certificate makes him independently experienced.

steps.text: Continue supervised preparation and fitting using the drawing notebook and checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we could stop worrying about who had the newest app and get the work done. If the office made an invoice quicker, fine. I'd still need the drawing explained properly before I fitted anything unfamiliar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect our wages and bills to remain steady in that picture. Eight months saved gives the household room for a quiet patch, and there are other firms around if this one changes. Being a beginner doesn't mean every ordinary bill frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep doing the supervised preparation and fitting work. In the first plateau year I'd keep my notebook of drawings and corrections and ask for the checks I needed. I wouldn't spend household money on another tool or leave a good wage over office changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household, with ordinary frustration when something takes me two tries. I'd be glad to stay with familiar work and get better at it. I don't need a changing future to feel a day has been useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does needing help from a younger worker bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the younger worker to show me again. Pride isn't much use if a fitting ends up wrong. I'd rather the children saw me asking a sensible question than pretending I knew an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the reserve differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it available for an actual interruption or repair bill. That's our existing reserve, not a new saving choice made because AI stayed small. I wouldn't empty it to celebrate reassuring news.

say: I'd accept office changes while asking for **real teaching time** around a beginner's practical work.
I'd tell the firm **quicker paperwork** doesn't make my hands understand an unfamiliar task.
think: I expect **practical wages and hours** to hold while the firm still needs preparation and fitting on site.
A rushed senior worker could mean **less useful teaching**, even while our own household bills remain covered.
do: Record jobs missing **checking time** in a paper notebook now.
Use the examples to request **paid supervised practice** during the first year, without a wage reduction.
feel: **Uneasy** about being hurried, while expecting the wage to hold and recognising present household security.
S1.quote: Quicker paperwork doesn't tell my hands what to do.
fieldNote: He locates **present discomfort** in teaching pressure rather than expected personal wage loss, keeping the mood tied to his own situation.
He requests **named supervised practice** without counting it as provided, and resists independent AI use even when office tools change.

steps.text: Continue familiar supervised work and record jobs missing required checking time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office could choose its tools, but it shouldn't book work as if a beginner learned at computer speed. I'd ask for enough time with the senior worker to understand the job. Quicker paperwork doesn't tell my hands what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my practical wage and hours to hold while the firm still needs materials prepared and fittings put in. But I would watch whether the senior worker got too rushed to teach me properly. Our own bills can be covered while the day becomes less comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep a paper note of jobs where the booked time didn't allow my needed checks. In the first year I'd take those examples to the supervisor and ask for a regular supervised practice period within paid hours, with no wage reduction. I wouldn't call the practice agreed until the firm confirmed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about being hurried, but not expecting to lose the wage in the next few years. I'd be irritated by another system telling me the work should already be done. I wouldn't confuse that irritation with an empty household account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an unfamiliar AI record tool became required?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask who would teach it and check the record during paid time. I wouldn't start using AI alone to look agreeable. The office being confident isn't the same as me understanding the task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful paid practice arrangement look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a named experienced worker to demonstrate, watch me repeat and check the result. I'd keep asking directly rather than leave a good wage in a temper. A paid learning arrangement would need to preserve the wage, not replace paid site hours.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking changes** from robots around 2031 and seek a paid apprenticeship route through the gap.
I wouldn't treat the **extra time** as a guarantee that a beginner receives proper teaching.
think: I could lose **paid hours** as firms prepare for robots and keep more work with stronger electricians.
Eight months of **bills saved** allows a careful search, without replacing the mortgage contribution for the rest of my career.
do: Ask the old instructor about **paid adult apprenticeships** with real supervised teaching now.
Accept an **apprenticeship place** before 2028 only with supervision and written wages covering bills after travel.
Apply after 2028 for **junior repair jobs** on those terms, remaining here until a signed offer exists.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with enough savings and local options to respond carefully.
S2.quote: Family responsibility means checking the actual money before making the promise.
fieldNote: His **apprenticeship condition** protects supervised teaching and livable written wages after travel rather than assuming a free course is affordable.
He remains **resistant to AI** while acknowledging real evidence of robots would strengthen the need to inspect paid alternatives.

steps.text: Take supervised paid apprenticeship before 2028 only with written wages covering bills after travel
Seek posted supervised repair jobs after 2028 with written bill-covering wages after travel before leaving
Keep current job until an affordable supervised offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking work changes in 2028 before the hands-on robots around 2031. I'd still want a paid apprenticeship route through that gap. The gap gives a beginner time to learn, not a guarantee somebody will teach him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose hours as firms prepared for robots and kept the strongest workers busy. Eight months of bills gives us time to search, but it doesn't pay the mortgage for a whole remaining career. I'd worry about having to change before I'd properly learned this trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my old instructor about real paid adult apprenticeship places with supervised teaching. I'd accept one before 2028 only with a written wage that covered our bills after travel and with actual supervision. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted junior repair jobs on the same terms, staying here until another signed offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost income, though I wouldn't be short of money tomorrow. The reserve and nearby firms would let me be cautious. I'd still resent needing another route when I'd only just got into this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an apprenticeship workable for the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner the wage, hours, journey and supervision before accepting anything. If a place only offered an unpaid course, I'd keep looking while earning here. Family responsibility means checking the actual money before making the promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would change how seriously you took the later robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see a real job done with the awkward access and checks included. I wouldn't suddenly begin using AI because I saw that. I would take the need to find an affordable supervised place more seriously.

say: I'd use **five years** to request proper teaching while still paid, starting now rather than waiting for 2031.
I'd keep **robots around 2034** visible instead of treating extra preparation as a different end point.
think: I expect **practical work and pay** to hold over the next few years while I become more competent.
I would still dislike **later changes**, because unfamiliar methods take time even with savings and local options.
do: Request regular **paid supervised practice** now without losing wages.
Accept an **adult apprenticeship** before 2031 only with supervision and written wages covering bills after travel.
Seek a signed **supervised junior service offer** covering bills after travel before leaving after 2031.
feel: **Uneasy** about later career change, while secure about near-term bills and glad of time for repeated practice.
S3.quote: Another year on a payslip isn't automatically another year of skill.
fieldNote: The **longer timeline** changes his expected near-term income, without claiming that the eventual hands-on endpoint has weakened.
He tests **learning progress** through correctly performed work and retains the present wage until an affordable supervised offer is signed.

steps.text: Take supervised paid apprenticeship before 2031 only with written wages covering bills after travel
Seek signed supervised service offers after 2031 with written wages covering bills after travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should let a person learn properly while he still has a wage. I'd ask for that teaching now, not after the thinking work changed in 2031. I'd still keep the hands-on robots around 2034 in the picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I expect my practical work and pay to hold through more preparation years. The reserve could stay a reserve while I became more competent. I would still dislike the thought of changing direction again later, because new methods don't come quickly to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for regular supervised practice within paid work without a wage reduction. I'd accept a paid adult apprenticeship before 2031 only with supervision and written wages covering our bills after travel. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for junior service roles on the same basis, keeping this job until a signed offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later change, but secure about our own bills over the next few years. I'd feel better having time to repeat a practical task until I knew it. I wouldn't need to pretend I enjoyed every new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge progress during the extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what I could now do correctly with the required checks. If the answer stayed the same, I'd ask why the promised teaching hadn't happened. Another year on a payslip isn't automatically another year of skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm never provided the practice it talked about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the actual place and its wage rather than leave this firm in frustration. I wouldn't spend the reserve to prove I was serious about learning. I'd want a signed affordable offer before changing anything.

say: I'd use **ten years** for real teaching while asking for the next practical task now.
I'd prefer **one correctly learned task** to a long series of reassuring talks without paid practice.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I couldn't assume our current reserve meant we could stop earning when robots followed.
Present **pay and savings**, alongside many nearby firms, make the next few years' household bills look secure.
do: Request **paid supervised practice** without wage reduction and review the next practical skill each year.
Accept a supervised **paid apprenticeship** before 2036 only with written wages covering bills after travel.
Seek a signed **supervised repair offer** covering bills after travel before leaving after 2036.
feel: **Uneasy** about eventual change, while secure about near-term living and able to learn at a cautious pace.
S4.quote: A long warning doesn't replace somebody standing beside the learner.
fieldNote: He makes **no retirement assumption** from being in his fifties and refuses to treat children's future earnings as household resources.
His **annual check** turns promised teaching into a question about actual correctly performed work and usable paid alternatives.

steps.text: Take supervised paid apprenticeship before 2036 only with written wages covering bills after travel
Seek signed supervised repair offers after 2036 with written wages covering bills after travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is room to teach a trade properly, not a reason to keep postponing the teaching. I'd ask for the next practical task now. I'd rather have one thing I could actually do well than ten years of reassuring talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when thinking work changed in 2036 and around 56 when the robots followed. I couldn't assume we'd have enough to stop earning then just because we had a reserve now. Our present pay, savings and plenty of nearby firms would still make the next few years secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd request the same paid supervised practice with no wage reduction and review the next skill each year. I'd accept a supervised paid apprenticeship before 2036 only if written wages covered household bills after travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd seek a signed supervised repair offer on those terms before leaving the current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual change, but not afraid for our next household bills. I'd have room to learn slowly and still ask for checks. I wouldn't suddenly want to teach myself through a screen because the deadline moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the decade from becoming years of waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask yearly which tasks I could do correctly under the required checks and what paid work those skills opened. If teaching remained a promise, I'd compare actual supervised places sooner. A long warning doesn't replace somebody standing beside the learner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the longer picture change plans for the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't decide their studies from this card or count their future wages as ours. I'd tell them I was learning and that admitting a question was part of doing a proper job. I wouldn't ask them to be my retirement plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose hours before I had become a useful tradesman. A proper supervised paid apprenticeship with wages we could live on would help me do something real. Eight months of savings gives me time to ask carefully, not permission to pretend I know the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the person actually wants to learn from a screen. I want to work and improve, but I need the demonstration and the chance to repeat it with someone watching. Being cautious doesn't mean I don't care about earning my way.

headlineQuote: Eight months of savings gives me time to ask carefully, not permission to pretend I know the work.
portrait: **Colin, 43**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, high trade pay and practical skills still below the experienced crew's level.
He and **his partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage, eight months of expenses saved and many nearby electrical employers.
He **never uses AI**, preferring marked drawings, demonstration and repeated checks while valuing work, family responsibility and paid apprenticeships.
Fast competition threatens **junior hours**; slower preparation preserves near-term security without assumed retirement or children's earnings replacing future wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his hours before he becomes a useful tradesman.
whatWouldHelp: A **supervised paid apprenticeship** with livable household wages would let him learn through real work.
